content.intro: This lesson introduces Concurrency and Coordination Patterns using the supplied syllabus terms, a visual map, and a short inspectable example.
content.why_it_matters: Understanding Concurrency and Coordination Patterns helps you make JavaScript behavior explicit instead of relying on guesswork. The skill becomes more valuable as programs combine data, user input, runtime APIs, and failures.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Concurrency and Coordination Patterns is one of the named concepts in the JavaScript syllabus. Focus on the behavior it defines, the inputs that influence that behavior, and the result you can observe. JavaScript language semantics are specified by ECMAScript; browser and Node.js APIs belong to their host runtimes, so check which environment a feature requires.

content_blocks.title: Build the idea in small steps

items.title: Sequential versus concurrent tasks
items.text: Model Sequential versus concurrent tasks as an ordering and failure-handling problem. Identify what starts the work, how completion is signaled, and where rejection or cancellation is handled.

items.title: Running independent tasks together
items.text: Model Running independent tasks together as an ordering and failure-handling problem. Identify what starts the work, how completion is signaled, and where rejection or cancellation is handled.

items.text: Connect Coordinating shared state and results to Concurrency and Coordination Patterns. Define the expected behavior first, demonstrate it with a small example, and explain one edge case before using it in a larger program.

content_blocks.title: Environment and correctness note
content_blocks.text: The ECMAScript 2026 edition is the stable language reference used by this course. The browser DOM, Fetch API, and Node.js APIs are host features. Emerging proposals and runtime support can change; verify compatibility before depending on a feature in production.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without understanding its input and output.
common_mistakes.why: A memorized example can appear to work while hiding assumptions about input values or runtime.
common_mistakes.fix: Explain the expected output first, run the smallest example, and test one boundary case.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming browser APIs are part of core JavaScript.
common_mistakes.why: ECMAScript does not define the browser DOM or Node.js filesystem APIs.
common_mistakes.fix: Identify the host environment and consult its official API reference.

common_mistakes.why: Several simultaneous edits make the cause of a behavior difficult to isolate.
common_mistakes.fix: Change one variable or line, reproduce the result, and record what changed.
